edges.effect_quant: Prospective studies are mostly near null overall, although some pooled analyses report lower colon-cancer risk at higher intake levels.
edges.mechanism: Coffee can alter bile-acid metabolism, colonic motility, insulin signaling, and microbial fermentation, which makes a colorectal effect biologically plausible. The problem is that these pathways do not translate into one stable epidemiologic pattern across colon and rectal cancer or across populations.
edges.summary: This is another edge where the literature refuses to settle into a single answer. Two recent prospective syntheses found no clear overall association with colorectal-cancer incidence, while an earlier meta-analysis suggested lower risk at higher intake and a more visible signal for colon than rectal cancer.
edges.caveats: Results vary by tumor subsite, sex, smoking status, and geography, which makes pooled overall estimates look cleaner than the underlying data really are. Any protective effect, if present, is probably small and not a reason to frame coffee as a colorectal-prevention tool.

evidence.citation: Micek A et al 2019 Int J Food Sci Nutr
